title: נחום איש גם זו

paragraphs: Naḥum of Gam Zu. Arukh, Gamzu: some explain a place-name; II Chronicles 28 has a place Gamzo. Ta'avah LaEinayim writes that Chronicles spells Gimzo with yod, whereas here it has pataḥ, hence they expound 'This too is for good.' Moreover, since it says 'man of Gam Zu' rather than Naḥum Gamzo, perhaps he came from the town Gamzo. Yuḥasin forgot to include him alphabetically among the tannaim. He was Akiva's teacher for twenty-two years, Ḥagigah 12a; Shevuot 26a; Bereshit Rabbah 23 [digital parallel: 1:14]. Berakhot 22a: '[Naḥum] whispered it to Akiva.' He was accustomed to miracles, Ta’anit 20a [digital text: 21a] and Ḥelek, ר״ח [digital parallel: Sanhedrin 108b–109a]; see his wondrous deeds. He said, 'This too is for good,' hence Gam Zu. His student Akiva likewise said everything done from Heaven is for good (see his entry). R. Yishmael served him. Gilgulei Neshamot (ג״נ) writes that Naḥum of Gam Zu was an ibbur of Lot (bearing Lot’s soul): in the Ta'anit incident, dirt replaced his stolen gold, and the king conquered a province with that dirt; likewise Abraham's sword was dirt when he rescued Lot. His hands and feet were cut off because he had not shown compassion in Sodom: 'They did not strengthen the poor and needy's hand,' as in Ta'anit and Jerusalem Talmud, end of Pe'ah. Lot escaped Sodom and it immediately overturned; here too the house collapsed as soon as Naḥum left. Thus he said he was assured it would not fall while he remained inside, like the angel saying, 'I cannot do anything until you arrive there.' End of quotation. At Rafadya Naḥum of Gam Zu is buried beneath a monument; below him is R. Yishmael's grave—גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael].
